questions.question: What is S3 Static Website Hosting and when would you use it?
questions.answer: S3 Static Website Hosting is a feature of Amazon S3 that lets you serve a static website directly from a bucket — no servers, no Apache, no infrastructure management. You use it when your website consists of pre-built HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and image files with no server-side processing. It is ideal for portfolio sites, documentation, landing pages, and company brochure websites. Compared to EC2, it requires zero infrastructure management, scales automatically, and you pay only for storage used and data transferred.

questions.question: What are the steps to host a static website on S3?
questions.answer: Five steps: (1) Create an S3 bucket with a globally unique name. (2) Upload all website files — HTML, CSS, JS, images — directly to the bucket root, not inside folders. (3) Go to Properties, enable Static Website Hosting, and set the Index document (e.g., index.html) and Error document. (4) Go to Permissions, disable Block Public Access. (5) Add a bucket policy with Effect Allow, Principal *, Action s3:GetObject, Resource bucket-ARN/*. Once both steps 4 and 5 are done, the website URL will work.

questions.question: Why does disabling Block Public Access alone not make an S3 bucket website accessible?
questions.answer: Disabling Block Public Access removes the guardrail that prevents public permissions from being applied — but it does not itself grant any permission. A bucket policy must also be added that explicitly allows s3:GetObject for Principal * (everyone). Think of it as: Block Public Access is a master lock that prevents any public rules from taking effect. Disabling it opens the door, but you still need a rule (bucket policy) saying who can enter.

questions.question: What is a CDN and why is it important for global websites?
questions.answer: A CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a globally distributed network of servers — called edge locations — that cache content near users to deliver it faster. Without a CDN, all users globally must send requests to your origin server (e.g., an S3 bucket in Mumbai), causing high latency for distant users. With a CDN, content is cached at edge locations near each user. A user in Germany gets content from a Frankfurt edge location instead of Mumbai — reducing latency from seconds to milliseconds. CDNs also reduce load on the origin server.

questions.question: What is Amazon CloudFront and what is a distribution?
questions.answer: Amazon CloudFront is AWS's managed CDN service. It delivers web content with low latency and high transfer speeds using a global network of edge locations. A distribution is the CloudFront configuration — it specifies your origin (where your content lives), caching settings, security options, and the root document to serve. You share the distribution's domain name (e.g., xyz.cloudfront.net) with your users instead of the origin URL.

questions.question: What is Origin Access Control (OAC) and why should you use it?
questions.answer: OAC (Origin Access Control) is a CloudFront security feature that grants a specific CloudFront distribution permission to access a private S3 bucket. Instead of making the bucket public, you keep Block Public Access enabled and let OAC handle authentication. When you enable OAC, CloudFront auto-generates a bucket policy that allows only cloudfront.amazonaws.com from your specific AWS account and distribution ID to read objects. This means the bucket stays private — the general public cannot access it directly via the S3 URL — but CloudFront can still serve the content globally.

questions.question: What is the difference between an edge location and an AWS Availability Zone?
questions.answer: An edge location (also called a Point of Presence) is a small CDN caching node used by CloudFront to serve cached content near users. There are hundreds of edge locations globally. An Availability Zone (AZ) is a full data center cluster within an AWS Region, hosting EC2, RDS, S3, and other compute/storage services. Edge locations are CDN-specific for content delivery. AZs are for hosting applications and data. They are completely separate concepts — edge locations do not run your EC2 instances.

questions.question: What is TTL in CloudFront caching, and what are the trade-offs of short vs long TTL?
questions.answer: TTL (Time to Live) is how long a CloudFront edge location keeps a cached copy of content before checking the origin for updates. Short TTL (e.g., 60 seconds) means content is refreshed more frequently — users see updates sooner but the origin gets more requests. Long TTL (e.g., 86400 seconds / 24 hours) maximizes caching — origin gets fewer requests and performance is optimal, but users may see stale content after updates. The right TTL depends on how frequently your content changes.

questions.question: Why should you use the S3 bucket name instead of the website endpoint URL as the CloudFront origin?
questions.answer: When you use the website endpoint URL as the CloudFront origin, the S3 bucket MUST be publicly accessible — which defeats the purpose of CloudFront for security. But when you use the bucket name as the origin and enable OAC, the bucket can remain completely private. CloudFront authenticates to S3 using the OAC mechanism. The general public cannot access the bucket URL directly; they can only access content via CloudFront. This gives you both security (private bucket) and global performance (CDN).

questions.question: What are the three most important settings when creating a CloudFront distribution for S3 static website hosting?
questions.answer: Three essential settings: (1) Origin — set to your S3 bucket NAME (not the website endpoint URL). (2) OAC (Origin Access Control) — enable this so CloudFront can access a private bucket. CloudFront will auto-generate and apply a bucket policy. (3) Default Root Object — set to index.html (or your main page filename). This tells CloudFront which file to serve when users visit the root URL of the distribution. Without the root object setting, visiting the distribution URL shows an error instead of your homepage.

questions.question: Describe a scenario where you solved a real-world latency and security problem using CloudFront.
questions.answer: (Situation) A client in Singapore deployed a static website on S3 in the Mumbai region with a public bucket and website endpoint URL. Customers globally complained of slow load times, and the security team flagged the bucket as publicly accessible. (Task) Resolve both latency and security issues without taking the site offline. (Action) Created a CloudFront distribution using the S3 bucket name (not website URL) as origin, enabled OAC, let CloudFront auto-generate the bucket policy, re-enabled Block Public Access to make the bucket private, and set index.html as the default root object. (Result) The website now loads fast for global users via edge locations, the S3 bucket is completely private, and direct S3 URL access returns 403 Forbidden — both problems solved simultaneously.

questions.question: A user updates website files in S3 but CloudFront customers still see old content. Walk through the diagnosis and fix.
questions.answer: (Situation) Website content was updated in S3 but customers globally still see the old version. (Task) Restore the correct content visibility for all users immediately. (Action) Diagnosed the issue as CDN caching — edge locations still served the cached version because TTL had not expired. Created a CloudFront cache invalidation for /* (all files) to force all edge locations to discard their cached copies. Verified by testing the CloudFront URL after the invalidation completed. (Result) All users saw the updated content within minutes, without waiting for TTL to expire naturally.

questions.question: Your manager asks whether to use S3 Static Website Hosting or EC2 to host a brochure website. How do you advise?
questions.answer: (Situation) The company needs to host a simple brochure website (HTML, CSS, images — no backend). (Task) Recommend the right AWS hosting solution. (Action) Recommended S3 Static Website Hosting for three reasons: (1) Zero infrastructure management — no EC2 to launch, patch, or maintain. (2) Cost — EC2 charges 24x7 even with no traffic; S3 charges only for storage used and data transferred. (3) Simplicity — upload files, enable feature, done. Reserved EC2 only for dynamic sites with backend logic, databases, or server-side code. (Result) The brochure site was deployed in under 30 minutes with no server management overhead.

questions.question: Security team flags the S3 bucket as publicly accessible. How do you close this security gap while keeping the website live?
questions.answer: (Situation) A static website runs on S3 with a public bucket (Block Public Access disabled, public bucket policy). Security team raised a flag. (Task) Make the bucket private while keeping the website accessible to customers. (Action) Created a CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket name as origin and OAC enabled. CloudFront auto-generated a private bucket policy. Re-enabled Block Public Access on S3 to make the bucket private. Removed the old public bucket policy. Updated customer-facing URL to the CloudFront distribution domain. (Result) The website remains fully accessible through CloudFront; direct S3 URL now returns 403 — the bucket is completely private as required by security policy.

questions.question: How does a CDN handle the first request vs. subsequent requests for the same file?
questions.answer: (Situation) A CDN is configured in front of an S3 origin. (Task) Explain cache miss and cache hit behavior. (Action) First request from a new region: cache miss — the edge location has no cached copy, so it fetches from the S3 origin (Mumbai), caches the file according to the TTL setting, and serves it to the user. Second and subsequent requests from the same region: cache hit — the edge location has the cached copy and serves it instantly without contacting origin. (Result) Only the first request incurs the full round-trip latency; all subsequent requests are served locally from the edge, dramatically reducing load times and origin traffic.

questions.question: What is an OAI (Origin Access Identity) and how does it differ from OAC?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team asks whether to use OAI or OAC for a new CloudFront + S3 setup. (Task) Explain the difference and make a recommendation. (Action) OAI (Origin Access Identity) is the older CloudFront mechanism for giving CloudFront access to a private S3 bucket. OAC (Origin Access Control) is the newer, recommended replacement. Key differences: OAC supports SSE-KMS encrypted S3 buckets; OAI does not. OAC conditions in bucket policies include the account ID and distribution ARN for stronger access control. AWS officially recommends OAC for all new distributions. (Result) Recommended OAC for all new setups. Existing OAI setups should be migrated to OAC to support encryption and improve security posture.

questions.question: A colleague points their CloudFront distribution at your private S3 bucket. Will it work?
questions.answer: (Situation) A colleague from a different team creates a CloudFront distribution targeting your private S3 bucket without your knowledge. (Task) Determine if this will work and explain why. (Action) With OAC in place, the S3 bucket policy includes a condition specifying AWS:SourceAccount (your account ID) and AWS:SourceArn (your distribution's ARN). Any request from a different distribution or account will not match this condition — S3 will deny the request. (Result) The colleague's distribution cannot access your bucket. OAC ensures that only your specific CloudFront distribution from your specific AWS account can read objects — providing strong access isolation.

questions.question: Walk through all the EC2 setup steps that S3 Static Website Hosting eliminates.
questions.answer: (Situation) A junior developer argues EC2 is just as easy as S3 for a static site. (Task) Clarify the operational difference. (Action) For EC2 you must: (1) Choose and launch an instance with the right AMI and instance type. (2) Attach and configure storage (EBS). (3) SSH in and install Apache HTTPD or Nginx. (4) Configure the web server and set up virtual hosts. (5) Deploy website files to the web server directory. (6) Set up Auto Scaling Groups if you expect traffic spikes. (7) Set up an Application Load Balancer and target groups. (8) Manage OS patching and security updates ongoing. (9) Pay 24x7 for running instances. S3 skips all of these — just upload files, enable static hosting, configure permissions. (Result) S3 is dramatically simpler and cheaper for static content.

questions.question: What happens to the S3 website endpoint URL after you switch to CloudFront with OAC?
questions.answer: After configuring CloudFront with OAC and re-enabling Block Public Access, the S3 static website endpoint URL (e.g., bucket.s3-website.region.amazonaws.com) returns 403 Access Denied. This is expected and desired — the bucket is now private and only CloudFront can access its objects via OAC. Customers should use the CloudFront distribution domain name (e.g., xyz.cloudfront.net) instead. The website is still accessible, just through a different — and more secure and performant — URL.

questions.question: Describe how you would verify that a CloudFront + S3 OAC setup is working correctly after deployment.
questions.answer: (Situation) A CloudFront distribution with OAC has just been created and deployed. (Task) Verify the setup is correct. (Action) Perform three tests: (1) Open the CloudFront distribution domain (xyz.cloudfront.net) in a browser — the website should load correctly with all pages and images. This confirms CloudFront can access S3 via OAC and the default root object is configured. (2) Open the S3 static website endpoint URL directly — it should return 403 Forbidden. This confirms the bucket is private. (3) Check the S3 bucket policy under Permissions — it should show the auto-generated OAC policy with cloudfront.amazonaws.com as Principal and your account/distribution conditions. All three tests passing confirms correct setup.

questions.question: How would you architect a globally available, secure, and cost-optimized static website on AWS?
questions.answer: Optimal architecture: (1) Create a private S3 bucket in a single region (e.g., us-east-1) to store website files. No need for multi-region buckets — CloudFront handles global delivery. (2) Enable S3 versioning for rollback capability. (3) Create a CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket name as origin. Enable OAC. Set index.html as the default root object. Configure an appropriate TTL (e.g., 86400 for stable content, lower for frequently changing content). (4) Optionally enable CloudFront cache invalidation automation triggered by S3 deployment updates. (5) Use Route 53 to map a custom domain to the CloudFront distribution using an Alias record. (6) Enable HTTPS via AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) on the CloudFront distribution. Result: globally fast (edge caching), secure (private bucket, HTTPS), cost-optimized (single S3 bucket, CDN reduces origin hits), and professional (custom domain).

questions.question: Explain the complete security model of CloudFront + S3 with OAC. Who can access what?
questions.answer: The security model has three layers: (1) S3 bucket is PRIVATE — Block Public Access is enabled. No one on the public internet can access objects via the S3 URL or any other mechanism except through authorized principals. (2) OAC bucket policy — the only entity allowed to read objects is cloudfront.amazonaws.com from your specific AWS account AND your specific distribution ARN. Even if someone creates a different CloudFront distribution and points it at your bucket, the condition block in the policy rejects them. (3) CloudFront distribution — only serves content from the origin (S3) to users. Users access the CloudFront domain (xyz.cloudfront.net). Direct S3 URL access returns 403. This layered model means: the general public can access your website only through CloudFront, and CloudFront itself can access S3 only through the tightly scoped OAC policy.

questions.question: How does caching in CloudFront reduce costs in addition to improving performance?
questions.answer: CloudFront reduces costs in two ways: (1) Reduced S3 data transfer costs — every request that hits an edge location cache (cache hit) does NOT reach the S3 origin. S3 charges for data transferred out. If 90% of requests are cache hits, you pay 90% less S3 data transfer fees. (2) Reduced S3 request costs — S3 charges per GET request. With high cache hit rates, CloudFront dramatically reduces the number of GET requests hitting S3. The trade-off is CloudFront charges for data transferred from edge locations and per HTTP request — but for high-traffic sites, the CDN pricing is usually lower than the S3 savings. For low-traffic sites, the Free Tier (1 TB + 10M requests/month) covers most needs.

questions.question: What happens if you forget to set the Default Root Object in a CloudFront distribution?
questions.answer: If no Default Root Object is set, accessing the root URL of the distribution (e.g., https://xyz.cloudfront.net/) will not return your index.html — CloudFront will return a 403 Access Denied or 403/404 error because it tries to access the root of the bucket without a specific key name. The website only works if users access specific file paths directly (e.g., xyz.cloudfront.net/index.html). Setting Default Root Object to index.html tells CloudFront to automatically serve index.html when the root URL is accessed — making the website behave as expected.

questions.question: Compare S3 Transfer Acceleration and CloudFront — when would you use each?
questions.answer: These services address opposite directions of data transfer. S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations to accelerate file UPLOADS from users to S3. When a user uploads a large file, it goes to the nearest edge location which routes it to S3 over AWS's optimized backbone network — faster than the public internet. You use Transfer Acceleration when users globally need to upload large files to a centralized S3 bucket quickly. CloudFront, on the other hand, accelerates DOWNLOADS — caching content at edge locations so users globally get fast reads. You use CloudFront when serving website content, images, videos, or APIs to global users. For a website serving files to customers, use CloudFront. For an application that lets users upload files to S3, use Transfer Acceleration.
